note: Prose. Dante's Italian says "loosened words", words freed from meter and rhyme. Even prose, which can say anything, could not do justice to this sight, and he must tell it in verse.
Puglia, or Apulia, here means the whole south of mainland Italy. Dante piles up five wars fought there over fifteen centuries, and says all their wounded together would not match this one ditch.
Dante's Italian says "Trojans", meaning the Romans, who traced their descent from Aeneas and his Trojans. The wars are usually taken to be Rome's early conquest of southern Italy.

The Second Punic War (218–201 BC), and above all the battle of Cannae in Apulia in 216 BC, where Hannibal destroyed a Roman army. The gold rings taken from the Roman dead were sent to Carthage and poured out in a heap before its senate.
Roman historian (59 BC–AD 17), whose history of Rome tells the story of the rings. "Without error" is Dante's tribute to him as the great authority on Rome's past.

Norman adventurer (about 1015–1085) who conquered southern Italy from the Byzantine Greeks and the Saracens and became duke of Apulia and Calabria. Dante places him in Heaven among the warriors of the faith (Paradiso 18).

A river crossing on the border of the kingdom of Naples. In 1266 the barons of the south, who should have held it for King Manfred, let the invader Charles of Anjou pass. The battle itself was fought soon after at Benevento, where Manfred was killed. Dante meets him in Purgatorio 3.

In 1268 Charles of Anjou defeated Conradin, the last heir of the imperial Hohenstaufen house, near this town in the Abruzzi. Alardo is Érard de Valéry, an old French knight. On his advice Charles kept a reserve hidden until the enemy scattered to plunder: a victory by cunning, not by arms.

context: The ninth of the ten ditches holds the sowers of discord: those who split apart religions, cities and families.

note: After the grand roll call of battles, the language drops on purpose to the tavern and the butcher's stall: a broken barrel, guts, excrement. Dante matches a low style to a degraded sight.

context: Dante places him here as a schismatic, not as the founder of another religion: in the medieval Christian view he had torn a great part of the world away from the Church. His body is split as he was held to have split the faith.

note: Cousin and son-in-law of Mohammed, and the fourth caliph (died 661). The quarrel over his right to lead divided Islam into Sunni and Shia. His wound completes Mohammed's: one is split from chin to groin, the other from chin to hairline.
Scandal here means discord, the setting of people against one another. The punishment fits the sin exactly: those who divided what should be whole are themselves divided.
The souls walk around the ditch in a ring. At one point stands a devil with a sword who cuts each of them open again as they pass.
The healing is part of the punishment. Each time around the ditch the wound has closed, so the sword always has whole flesh to cut.
Dante and Virgil stand on the stone bridge that arches over the ditch and look down. Mohammed takes Dante for a dead soul putting off his own sentence.

context: Virgil answers for Dante, as he often does: this man is alive, and is here to learn, not to be punished.

note: Leader of the Apostolic Brethren, a sect of northern Italy that preached holding all goods in common and was condemned as heretical. Mohammed's warning to him is mocking fellow feeling, from one splitter of the Church to another.

The men of Novara, in northern Italy. The pope proclaimed a crusade against Dolcino, who held out with his followers in the mountains until hunger and the winter snows forced them to surrender in 1307. He was burned at the stake that year. The poem is set in 1300, so this is "prophecy" written after the event.
The soul claims to have seen Dante in Italy. Nothing is known of any meeting between them.

Medicina is a town between Bologna and Imola. Almost nothing is known of Pier beyond this passage. Early commentators say he made trouble among the lords of Romagna, carrying tales that set one against another.
The whole plain of the river Po, from Vercelli in Piedmont in the west to Marcabò, a Venetian fortress near the river's mouths, in the east.

Guido del Cassero and Angiolello da Carignano, leading men of Fano, a town on the Adriatic coast. The murder foretold here is known only from Dante and his early commentators, who place it some years after 1300.
A town on the Adriatic coast between Rimini and Fano.
From one end of the Mediterranean to the other.
The Roman god of the sea.
Dante's word is "Argolic", from Argos: the Greeks, who had an old reputation as raiders of the sea.
Malatestino Malatesta, lord of Rimini, known as "Malatestino of the Eye" because he had lost one. He is the younger of the two mastiffs of Rimini in Inferno 27.
Rimini. The soul who wishes he had never seen it is Curio, pointed out a few lines below. It was at Rimini that he gave the advice that damned him.

Focara is a headland on the coast near Cattolica, feared for its sudden winds. Sailors rounding it made vows and prayers for safety. The two men will need none: they will be drowned before they reach it.
Dante picks up Pier's riddle: who is the one for whom the sight of Rimini was so bitter?

context: In January of 49 BC Caesar stood with his army near Rimini, at the river Rubicon, the border he was forbidden to cross under arms. Crossing it began the civil war that ended the Roman Republic.

note: Dante is paraphrasing a line the Roman poet Lucan gives to Curio in his epic on the civil war, the Pharsalia: delay always harms those who are ready.

Gaius Scribonius Curio, a Roman tribune who went over to Caesar's side and was driven from Rome. In Lucan he joins Caesar at Rimini and urges him to march on. The tongue that gave the advice is cut out. Dante elsewhere defends Caesar's cause, but here the counsel that started a civil war is a sin.

context: In Inferno 6, Dante asked after Mosca as one of the worthy Florentines of an earlier day, and was told he lay deeper in Hell. Here he finds him.

note: A Florentine proverb, in Italian "Capo ha cosa fatta": a thing done has an end. With it Mosca argued that a man who had insulted the Amidei family should be killed outright, not merely beaten. The hands that helped do the killing are cut off.

context: Florentine chroniclers dated the city's split into the two parties from the murder Mosca urged, about 1215. The feud spread through Tuscany and lasted the rest of the century.

note: Dante adds to Mosca's pain on purpose. The Lamberti were Ghibellines, and were banished from Florence with the rest of their party in Dante's childhood.
Before the hardest thing to believe in the canto, Dante stops to swear that he saw it. A clear conscience, he says, is like a coat of mail.
The eyes are in the head, so the body carries the head in front of it to see the way, as a walker at night carries a lamp.

context: Dante admired his poetry and elsewhere praises his generosity. That does not save him: he is damned for setting a son against his father.

note: Henry (1155–1183), eldest son of Henry II of England. He was crowned in his father's lifetime, which gave him his nickname, then rebelled against him and died young without ever ruling.
King David's counselor in the Bible, who went over to David's son Absalom and urged him on in his revolt against his father. When his advice was set aside he hanged himself (2 Samuel 15–17).

context: His son Absalom rose against him and drove him from Jerusalem. Absalom was killed in the battle that followed, and David wept for him.

note: In Italian, "lo contrapasso": the only time the poem uses the word that readers now apply to all its punishments. It means suffering in return what one did. Bertran parted a father from his son, so his head is parted from his body.
